bio.en: Maya Prohovnik was Spotify's Head of Product for podcasting, where she oversaw the product that powered Anchor's rapid hosting growth.
bio.zh: 玛雅·普罗霍夫尼克（Maya Prohovnik）曾任 Spotify 的播客产品负责人，主管驱动 Anchor 快速获取托管市场份额的产品。

summary.en: Maya recounts how the team obsessively reduced friction by quietly having interns manually submit podcasts to Apple behind the scenes, creating a magical one-click experience. She explains this scrappy approach is what drove Anchor's explosive market-share growth. The episode is a lesson in hiding complexity to deliver seeming simplicity at scale.
summary.zh: 玛雅讲述团队如何痴迷于降低摩擦——悄悄让实习生在后台手动把播客提交到 Apple，从而造出"一键发布"的魔法体验。她说明，正是这种灵活务实的做法推动了 Anchor 托管市场份额的爆发式增长。本期是关于"隐藏复杂性、在规模上交付看似简单"的一课。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: We were obsessed with reducing friction, this was our constant battle. And so we hired a couple of college interns and we brought them in and we were like, people are going to push this magical one button in the Anchor app and they're going to say, I want to distribute my podcast, and your job is going to be to do all that same manual stuff manually, but to them it's going to feel magical and it happened automatically. I still don't know how many people know this. I think people think that we had some secret backdoor deal with Apple for distribution, but we just had college students making Apple podcast accounts and then submitting hundreds of thousands of podcasts through these accounts, and I think that was a really big part of why we got so much hosting market share so quickly because it was such an insane benefit over the other platforms which otherwise had been commoditized at that point.
turns.zh: 我们当时痴迷于减少摩擦，那是我们一直在打的仗。所以我们招了几个大学实习生，把他们带进来，然后我们说：人们会去按 Anchor app 里那个神奇的「一键」按钮，他们会说「我想分发我的播客」，而你的工作就是把那些原本要手动做的事全部手动完成，但对他们来说，它会感觉很神奇，像是自动发生的。我到现在都不确定有多少人知道这事。我想人们以为我们跟 Apple 在分发上有某种秘密后门协议，但其实我们只是让大学生去开 Apple 播客账号，然后通过这些账号提交成千上万个播客——而我认为，这正是我们那么快就拿下那么多托管市场份额的重要原因，因为相比当时已经商品化、毫无差异的其他平台，这优势太离谱了。

turns.speaker: Lenny

Today my guest is Maya Prohovnik. Maya is Spotify's head of product for podcasting where she oversees product design and engineering teams responsible for building the tools and experiences for podcasters and their listeners. Maya was also employee number one at Anchor, which Spotify acquired five years ago, which became the core of Spotify's podcasting hosting platform, which now powers over 75% of all new podcasts created in the world. In our conversation, we dig into why Maya is obsessed with dogfooding and why she encourages everyone on her team to create their own podcast. She's got four podcasts of her own, which are all very highly rated and people love. We dig into how she stays productive and organized in a very hectic senior leadership role, what she's done to allow for Anchor to continue to operate like a startup within a larger organization.

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Thank you so much for having me. You and I have been trying to get together for almost a year now.
turns.zh: 太感谢你邀请我了。你和我为了凑到一起，已经努力快一年了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. But it all worked out and it's going to be very worth it.
turns.zh: 哦天哪。不过总算成行了，而且绝对物超所值。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: You had a kid. I took parental leave.
turns.zh: 你之前有个孩子。我休了陪产假。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, right. That is true. Man, overlapping kid journeys. I also have been just really looking forward to this chat partly because you're amazing and partly because it just feels very meta to have the head of product of Spotify podcasting on the podcast, and I imagine many people are listening to this on Spotify, so there's this, I don't know, turtles all the way down situation happening.
turns.zh: 哦对，那是真的。老兄，咱俩的孩子历程重叠了。我也很期待这次聊天，一部分是因为你太厉害，一部分是因为——让 Spotify 播客业务的产品负责人来上播客，这感觉特别「元」（meta）。我想很多人大概是在 Spotify 上听这期的，所以这里有一种……我不知道，像是「乌龟套乌龟，一路套到底」的情形在发生。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I totally agree. I was thinking the same thing when I was preparing for it where it's like so much of what we have to talk about is so meta, and then we also have you and I know each other because you've been sending me feedback about the podcast experience on Spotify, so lots of circular stuff there.
turns.zh: 我完全同意。我在准备这期的时候也是这么想的——我们要聊的太多东西都好 meta，而且你我本来就认识，因为你一直在给我发关于 Spotify 上播客体验的反馈，所以那里有很多循环往复的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of Spotify and podcasting, clearly you've done an incredible job building podcasting on Spotify. From what I've read, it's the number one podcasting platform now. Is there a stat you could share by just the percentage of the market share essentially of Spotify podcasting?
turns.zh: 说到 Spotify 和播客，显然你把 Spotify 上的播客业务做得不可思议地好。据我所读，它现在是第一的播客平台了。有没有什么数据可以分享一下——比如 Spotify 播客在市场份额上大概占多少？

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I think we are now officially over a third of global market share of podcast listening, which is pretty insane.
turns.zh: 我想我们现在官方地已经超过了全球播客收听市场份额的三分之一，这挺疯的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is insane.
turns.zh: 那太疯了。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Also, I think on the hosting side, it's an even bigger number. Is there a stat you can share by just maybe new podcasts that are launched and how many are hosted on Spotify?
turns.zh: 还有，我觉得在托管这一侧，那个数字更大。有没有什么数据可以分享——比如新创建的播客里，有多少是在 Spotify 上托管的？

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Yeah, I think at this point it's more than 75% of all new shows on Spotify are hosted with Spotify for podcasters, which used to be Anchor. When we were acquired by Spotify, I think Anchor had already gotten to 40% of all new podcasts or something crazy. So, yeah.
turns.zh: 对，我想在这一点上，现在超过 75% 的 Spotify 上新节目，都是由「Spotify for Podcasters」（前身是 Anchor）托管的。被 Spotify 收购时，我想 Anchor 已经拿下了大概 40% 的所有新播客，或者某个惊人的数字。所以，对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Insane. Okay, so for these reasons, I want to spend the time that we have together unpacking how you operate as a product leader and essentially what you've learned about product org leadership growth and all those things. How's that sound?
turns.zh: 疯了。好，基于这些原因，我想把我们共处的时间，用来拆解你作为产品负责人是如何运转的，以及你从产品组织、领导力、增长等等这些事上，到底学到了什么。听起来怎么样？

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: That sounds perfect. My favorite topics.
turns.zh: 听起来完美。我最爱的话题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, let's do it. So as the first question I asked a PM who actually works for you, Wilma Chu, what to ask you, and the first thing that came to mind for her was this idea of dogfooding and how important dogfooding is to your way of operating as a product leader. As an example, you have three of your own podcasts on Spotify and I checked them out and they're all very highly rated, so they're not just like bullshit podcasts, they're real people actually listen and enjoy them. So my question to you is just why is dogfooding so important to you? How do you actually operationalize it? And then also maybe just talk about these podcasts that you have.
turns.zh: 好，那我们开始。作为第一个问题，我问了一位实际为你工作的 PM，Wilma Chu，该问你什么；而她脑子里冒出来的第一件事，就是「吃自己的狗粮」（dogfooding）这个点，以及它对你作为产品负责人的运转方式有多重要。举个例子，你在 Spotify 上有三档自己的播客，我去看过了，它们评分都很高，所以不是那种糊弄人的播客，是真正有听众在听、在享受的。所以我的问题是：为什么吃自己的狗粮对你这么重要？你实际上是怎么把它落到操作层面的？另外也聊聊你那些播客。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Sure. Well, I can talk about them forever, so be careful because I'll take up the whole hour with that. But I actually have four podcasts. There's two that I don't update as much anymore. So my first ever podcast was about Stephen King books. I'm a big Stephen King super fan. So, when I joined Anchor, and we weren't even fully podcasts yet, if you recall, we were something else audio, we were trying to avoid being podcasts for a while and then we decided to just be podcasts. But when I got into audio and trying to help audio creators, the first thing I did was make my own podcast because I was like, I know nothing about production or what it feels to even be a creator in that way.
turns.zh: 当然。这个我能聊到天荒地老，小心点，因为我会占掉整整一小时就聊这个。但我其实有四档播客。有两档我现在更新没那么勤了。我的第一档播客是关于 Stephen King 的小说的。我是个大 Stephen King 死忠粉。所以，当我加入 Anchor 时——那时我们都还没完全是「播客」，如果你记得的话，我们做的是别的音频东西，有一阵子我们刻意回避被称作播客，后来才决定就做播客。但当我要做音频、要去帮音频创作者时，我做的第一件事就是做了自己的播客，因为我想：我对制作一窍不通，也对「作为一个创作者到底是什么感觉」毫无概念。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And so I started my Stephen King podcast because that is the number one thing that I just love to talk about every day, which is one of my tips for podcasters. If you're trying to figure out what to make a show about, it's what can you talk about for? So I did that one for a while actually. I spent a ton of time editing it. I spent a ton of time on SEO and marketing it, and it got to the point, I think at its peak I was getting 5,000 listeners in a episode, which now seems small for a podcast, I know.
turns.zh: 于是我开了那档 Stephen King 播客，因为那是我每天最想聊的事——这也是我给播客主的一条建议。如果你想搞清楚要做档什么节目，就问：有什么是你聊起来能停不下来的？所以那档我其实做了一阵子。我花大量时间剪辑，花大量时间做 SEO 和推广，到巅峰时，我想单集大概有 5,000 个听众——现在看对一个播客来说似乎很小，我知道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, that's very legit.
turns.zh: 不，那已经很正经了。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Yeah, for a test podcast that I was just doing to learn how to do my job, I was so excited to get that audience and I fell off because, well, mostly I had a kid, I joined Spotify. My life's really busy and that level of production is so hard to do if it's not your full-time job, but I still get emails all the time from people who are like, please bring it back. I never found another great Stephen King because I really got deep into the books and the connection between the books. So that was one of them. The second one I did, still going today. So my husband and I have this Big Brother podcast, the show Big Brother, it's terrible.
turns.zh: 对，对于一档我只是用来学着怎么干自己活的测试播客来说，能拿到那样一批听众我超兴奋的；后来我停更了，主要是因为——嗯，主要是我有了孩子、又加入了 Spotify，生活真的太忙，而那种制作强度如果不是全职，真的很难维持。但我到现在还一直收到邮件，人们说「求你把它弄回来」。我之后再没找到另一个那么棒的 Stephen King 切入点，因为我真的钻进了那些书、以及书与书之间的联系里。所以那是其中一档。第二档我到现在还在做。就是我和我丈夫一起做的《Big Brother》播客——那档节目很烂。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I would not recommend listening to my podcast unless you are a Big Brother super fan, and I actually started that one because I wanted to get the other end of the spectrum where something we were really focused on with Anchor at the time was first time creators really growing the pie of podcasters and specifically we had this theory that podcast creation of the future would be mobile first and we had this really high-powered mobile app, and so I was like, I'm going to make a podcast that's fully mobile, not highly edited, not worry about making something that sounds like a traditional podcast. And I really leaned into all the Anchor features. So it's fully recorded on my phone. I do almost no editing, but I think the thing that's kept us going, because it's been six or seven years now we've been doing the show, it's really the community, the people who call in.
turns.zh: 除非你是《Big Brother》死忠粉，否则我不会推荐你听我的播客；而那档我当初开起来，是因为我想去试 Anchor 当时极度聚焦的另一端——我们当时有个理论：未来的播客创作会是「移动优先」的，而且我们有个火力很猛的移动 app。所以我就想：我要做一档完全在手机上完成的播客，不高强度剪辑、不追求听起来像传统播客。我真的把所有 Anchor 的功能都用透了。所以它全程用我手机录制，我几乎不剪辑；但我想，让我们坚持下来的，是已经六七年了的「社区」——是那些打进电话来的人。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I have no idea who these people are. I have no idea how they found this terrible show, but they love it. They call in every week. And that I think is one of the many things I've learned from dogfooding, a podcast creation app is that community piece is so important. If you don't know if anyone's listening, if you don't know what they like about it, if you don't know if they're coming back, it's so hard to keep investing the time. And then I made a show, my least known podcast, because it only got like 25 listeners for episode, it's about my favorite book of all time called Children of Time. It's actually a trilogy. And the reason it got almost no listeners is because there were tons of spoilers in the podcast and the book is like 800 pages long. So we were like, do not listen if you haven't read the book.
turns.zh: 我完全不知道这些人是谁。我也不知道他们是怎么找到这档烂节目的，但他们爱它。他们每周都打进来。而我想，那正是我从「吃自己的狗粮、用一个播客创作 app」这件事上学到的众多东西之一：那个社区的环节，实在太重要了。如果你不知道有没有人在听、不知道他们喜欢什么、不知道他们回不回来，就很难一直把时间投进去。后来我又做了一档我最不为人知的播客，因为单集大概只有 25 个听众——它是关于我有史以来最爱的书，《Children of Time》（时间之子），其实是个三部曲。它几乎没听众的原因是：节目里全是剧透，而那本书大概有 800 页长。所以我们当时说：还没读这本书的，千万别听。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: So, it was very niche, but I think it's a really good podcast if you've read Children of Time. And then my last one I just started doing a couple of years ago is about parenting. So I have a son who's two and a half now and we have been documenting our journey as parents all the way from, we went through IVF, so starting with sort of fertility, I have a really fun episode about childbirth if people are interested in that sort of thing. And then ever since then it's just been episodes about the transition to parenthood, which has not been particularly easy for us, and now my son's a toddler, so lots of fun things happening there. You're not there yet, but you will be and then you can listen to my toddler episodes.
turns.zh: 所以，它非常垂直小众；但如果你读过《Children of Time》，我想那真的是档好播客。然后我的最后一档，是几年前才开始的，关于育儿。我有个儿子，现在两岁半，我们从 IVF 一路走来，所以从生育之类的事开始，就把我们当父母的历程记录了下来；如果你对这类东西感兴趣，我有集特别好玩的关于生孩子的。从那以后，就一直是关于「过渡到为人父母」的各种集子——对我们来说这过程并不特别轻松——现在儿子是个小 toddler 了，所以那里有很多好玩的事发生。你还没到那步，但你会到的，到时你就能听我的 toddler 集了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I got to listen to the next... A few months ahead to learn from what you've learned.
turns.zh: 对。我算是提前几个月，从你学到的东西里先听为快了。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Yes, I think that's a good tactic.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得那是个好策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before we talk about dogfooding, have you ever considered going full-time on this stuff? This is always an option for people and clearly you've done great. At least two podcasts are killing it.
turns.zh: 在聊吃自己的狗粮之前，你有没有考虑过全职做这行？这对很多人一直是个选项，而且显然你做得很好。至少两档播客都在大杀四方。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I have not. And I think it's so funny because with my parenting podcast too, and even my terrible Big Brother podcast, I get compliments all the time and people are like, "I love listening to this." And my husband also is a really funny and a really good podcaster, but I don't know why I don't think of myself as a creator. I think to me it still feels like this exercise where it's like I'm making my podcast, but I'm really doing it so that I can learn about our product and get in the mindset of a creator. So I think the problem is I'm just too much of a product person. It's a means to an end for me instead of the end itself. But that is an interesting question because I know most people who podcasts, their ultimate goal is obviously to be able to do it full-time and that is interesting that I haven't thought about it.
turns.zh: 我没有。我觉得这很好笑，因为我的育儿播客、甚至那档烂《Big Brother》播客，我都一直收到夸奖，人们说「我好爱听这个」。而我丈夫也是个真的很有趣、很会做播客的人。但我不知道为什么，我不把自己当成一个创作者。我想对我来说，它依然更像是一种练习——就像：我在做我的播客，但我做它，其实是为了能理解我们的产品、进入创作者的心态。所以我想，问题出在我「产品人」的属性太强了。它是我达到目的的手段，而不是目的本身。不过这是个有意思的问题，因为我知道大多数做播客的人，他们终极目标显然就是能全职做这个——而我居然从没想过这点，挺有趣的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have a good backup plan of things if anything goes off the rails.
turns.zh: 你这算是给自己留了条后路，万一哪天翻车了还有东西靠。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I guess so, yeah.
turns.zh: 我想是吧，对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. Just coming back to this idea of dogfooding, where does that come from for you? What have you learned about just how to execute that?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好。回到「吃自己的狗粮」这个点，它对你是从哪儿来的？你从「怎么去执行它」这件事上，学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: It's just always been my natural state. I've had a handful of different product jobs and I guess they've all been tangentially related to helping creators or creative people. And so I think for me it's like I don't know how you can build those tools if you don't understand that mindset. I'm not surprised that it came to Wilma's mind when you asked her what to ask me because I am constantly yelling at my product team who do not have podcasts and being like, I really don't think that you can build the right things. If they talk to users all the time, they see the data, but all of them, once they finally start doing their podcast, they're like, I get it. Something clicked and now I feel like I really understand what they need. And I guess building tools for creators is similar to building a B2B product where you really have to understand business, it's their livelihood.
turns.zh: 这向来就是我的天然状态。我做过好几份不同的产品工作，我想它们全都多少跟「帮创作者或创意人」沾点边。所以对我来说，就像：如果你不理解那种心态，我都不知道你怎么造得出那些工具。当我问 Wilma 该问我什么时，她脑子里蹦出这个，我一点也不意外——因为我成天对我的产品团队吼，那些没有播客的人，我会说：我真的不觉得你们能造出对的东西。如果他们一直在跟用户谈，他们看得到数据，但等他们终于自己做起播客，他们就会说：我懂了。某个东西「咔嗒」一声对上了，而现在我觉得自己真的理解他们要什么了。而我想，为创作者造工具，有点像做 B2B 产品——你真的得理解「生意」，因为那是他们的生计。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And so I think if you're just looking at a list of feature requests, you're not necessarily going to prioritize it in the same way as if you deeply feel those problems. And I think for me, I don't know if I mentioned this to you, but when I first got into tech, I started in customer support, that was how I got into product, and so I think I just am a very user focused product person. I think there's different schools of thought for product and for me it's always been about making people happy, making their experience better, solving real problems in their lives. And so for me, becoming one of the users, I think it's made it so much easier for me to advocate for that being a pretty big chunk of the roadmap.
turns.zh: 所以我想，如果你只是看着一份功能需求清单，你未必会以跟「深切体会过那些问题」时同样的方式去排优先级。而且我想，对我来说——我不知道我有没有跟你提过——我刚入行做科技时，是从客户支持做起的，我就是那样进入产品圈的；所以我想我天生就是个极度以用户为中心的产品人。关于产品的思路有不同流派，而对我而言，一向都是关于「让人开心、让他们的体验更好、解决他们生活里真实的问题」。所以对我来说，成为用户中的一员，让「把这一大块写进路线图」变得容易太多了。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I think if you don't have that, especially coming from someone in leadership, it's so easy to just fall into that trap of like, well, we're working on the next big strategic thing, which is two years away, and then in the meantime your users are getting no value and then they're just going somewhere else. So I don't know. I think it's really important to me. It makes sense to me and also, I'm not sure how else I would do product. I've never really not done it that way. It
turns.zh: 我想，如果你没有这个，尤其当一个领导者时，太容易掉进那种陷阱：嗯，我们在搞下一个大的战略级东西，那玩意儿两年后才来；而在此期间，你的用户一点价值都没拿到，然后他们就跑去别处了。所以我不知道。我觉得它对我真的很重要。它对我讲得通；而且除此之外，我也不知道还能怎么去做产品。我从来没真正换过一种方式。它——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Reminds me of Airbnb Brian was a huge advocate on the host side of the product is like, you need to be a host, but many people couldn't because they didn't have a place that could be hosted. Is there anything you've learned about just how to make this a thing that actually works effectively, a way to operationalize this for people listening, they're like, "Oh, I should start encouraging my team to do?"
turns.zh: 这让我想起 Airbnb 的 Brian，他可是「宿主侧产品」的超级鼓吹者——就像，你得自己当宿主；但很多人做不到，因为他们没有能拿来托管的地方。你有没有学到什么，关于怎么让这件事真正有效地运转、变成一种可以操作的方法，好让听众里的那些人也能学着去鼓励自己的团队做？

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I'm constantly reminding our team to do this. And then I think that also comes from the other people who are doing it. So we really elevate the people on our team who have their own podcasts, we help them tell their stories internally. Whenever we do an offsite or any team activity, we'll always incorporate podcast creation or some way of making sure everyone on the team is using the tools. I don't know, I think a lot of it just comes from, I'm so vocal about this stuff. The other night I was recording a podcast and I DMed one of the engineers on our team and told him about this tiny little iOS bug and he was like, why are you DMing me about this at nine o'clock at night? I think I was also supposed to be on vacation, I can't remember.
turns.zh: 我一直在提醒我们的团队去做这件事。而我想，这也来自其他那些在做的人。所以我们真的会「拔高」团队里那些有自己播客的人，我们帮他们在内部讲出自己的故事。每次我们做 offsite 或任何团队活动，我们总会把「播客创作」或某种确保团队每个人都用上这些工具的方式，嵌进去。我不知道，我想很大一部分就是我在这类事上嗓门太大了。前两天晚上我在录播客，还 DM 了我们团队里的一个工程师，跟他说那个小小的 iOS bug；他就说：你大半夜九点 DM 我这个干嘛？我想我当时大概也应该在休假，记不清了。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: But then he got the bug fix the next day. And so I do think making that something that's really top of mind for the team that we do need to fix problems, that these things matter, I don't know. I always listen to the podcast that my team makes, so it's like I know they're going to get at least one listener. And then I think also I try, I think because I understand a big part of building tools for podcasters is understanding all the barriers to entry. It's actually a really difficult thing trying to get someone to put their voice out there, share their story, it's a really emotional journey. And so I feel like I've tried to turn some of the things that I've learned about podcasting into, I've never written it down, maybe I should, but I have a playbook that I'll tell people when they're considering making their own podcast.
turns.zh: 但第二天他就把 bug 修好了。所以我觉得，让「我们确实需要去修这些问题、这些东西很重要」成为团队脑子里排在最前面的事，是管用的，我不知道。我永远在听我团队做的播客，所以就像：我知道他们至少会有一个听众。然后我想，我也尝试——因为我知道，为播客主造工具，很大一块是理解「所有那些进入的门槛」。让一个人把声音放出来、分享自己的故事，真的是一段很情绪化的旅程。所以我觉得，我把从播客里学到的一些东西，转化成了——我从没写下来过，也许该写——但我有一套「打法」，会告诉那些考虑做自己播客的人。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: So it's just things like don't try and record by yourself, find a friend. That's a much easier way to get into it or don't follow a script because then you're going to feel really awkward and uncomfortable and not feel good about it afterwards. Or don't just record a test thing for 30 seconds and publish it because you have to make yourself feel the pain that we're trying to understand in our users.
turns.zh: 所以那些东西就像：别试着自己一个人录，找个小伙伴。那是入行容易得多的办法；或者别照着稿子念，因为那样你会觉得特别尴尬、不舒服，事后也不会有好的感觉。或者，别只录个 30 秒的测试玩意儿就发布，因为你得让自己也体会到我们想在用户身上理解的那种「痛」。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's cool about that that could turn into just onboarding education, basically your experience of making a podcast informs how to help new podcasters become successful.
turns.zh: 这里面酷的地方在于，它能变成实质上就是「新人引导/教育」——你做播客的经验，反过来告诉你怎么帮新播客主成功。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Totally, yeah. And also this is less about dogfooding, but one of my favorite things is I'm always just trying to convince everyone I meet to start a podcast, that's just become my annoying thing. And so if I'm interviewing someone for a job or if I'm at a party and mingling with people, it's like somehow the conversation always turns to their passions and then I'm like, you should make a podcast about it. And then they're like, well, I can't. And then I work my way through all the reasons they say they can't do it, and then they go start a podcast. So I'm like one person at a time.
turns.zh: 完全对。而且这也跟吃狗粮关系不大了，但我最爱的事之一，就是我一直试图说服每个我遇到的人去开一档播客——这已经成了我那个招人烦的癖好。所以如果我面试一个人，或者在一个派对上跟人寒暄，话题总会不知怎么就拐到他们的热情所在，然后我就来一句：你该做个关于这个的播客。然后他们说：嗯，我不行。然后我就把他们说「不行」的理由一条条拆掉，然后他们就去开播客了。所以我就像是一次搞定一个人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see how you're growing the platform now.
turns.zh: 我懂你是怎么把平台做大的了。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Yes, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very unscalable, hands to hand combat at parties. I get it. Okay. One thing you mentioned about being maybe the only listen of your coworkers podcast reminds me there's this platform where you could find Spotify music that has never ever been played once and you could be their first play and just go through.
turns.zh: 非常「不可规模化」——派对上面对面的硬碰硬。我懂了。好。你提到，你是你同事播客「唯一听众」这件事，让我想起有个平台，你能找到那些从来没被播放过一次的 Spotify 音乐，然后你可以成为它们的第一次播放，就这么一路听过去。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: That is so cool.
turns.zh: 那太酷了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's very touching, right?
turns.zh: 挺动人的，对吧？

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Yes. I haven't seen that and now I'm like, how can we productize that for podcasters? That's such a cool thing.
turns.zh: 对。我没见过那个，而我现在就在想：我们怎么把它产品化，给播客主？那真是太酷的一件事了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Anyway, another area that I've heard you're really strong at and came up with Wilma and a few other people I talked to is you find a really good balance between being very data-driven and also very gut driven, and this is something a lot of product leaders try to get better at. And so I'm curious just what have you learned about try to find that balance and also is there an example of something where you went against the data and went with your gut and it worked out.
turns.zh: 总之，另一个我听说你特别强、而且 Wilma 和我聊过的几个人都提到的点，是你在「极度数据驱动」和「也极度凭直觉」之间，找到了一个非常好的平衡。这是很多产品负责人都想变得更强的东西。所以我好奇：你从「找这个平衡」这件事上学到了什么？有没有一个例子，是你逆着数据、跟着直觉走、而且最后成了的？

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: If you remember the old days of the internet, I feel like there was really this different way of thinking about product development where it was so much more about what felt good and what made you feel something as a user in that product. And so it's like we used to be a lot more playful I think with software. I think we used to put a lot more emphasis on things like delightful animations or fun little Easter eggs, and I am not sure when or where that got lost, but it feels like product management as a role has gotten formalized and become a little bit more scientific, I'm generalizing, but I think a lot of product managers can be so focused on using the right frameworks and making sure that they have the right roadmap and all of this stuff.
turns.zh: 如果你记得互联网的早期，我觉得那时关于产品开发，有一种真的很不一样的思路——更多是关于「什么用起来感觉好、作为用户在这个产品里能感受到什么」。所以就像，我们以前做软件，要俏皮得多。我想我们以前会把多得多的权重，放在像让人愉悦的动画、或者好玩的小彩蛋上；而我不知道是从何时、在何处丢掉了这个，但感觉上，产品经理这个角色已经变得太正式、有点太「科学」了——我在泛化啊，但我觉得很多产品经理会那么聚焦于「用对框架、确保路线图正确」以及这一大堆东西。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And then it's like you find yourself in this cycle where you're just building things to build them and not really thinking about the connection to the end user. I think data is amazing and I'm like, we have such an incredible insights team at Spotify, both my insights team and then the broader one. I think we are so lucky and we have so much knowledge about our users and different cohorts and what people need and what they're missing, and so I think that's extremely valuable. I think where people get into trouble is when they think that they can rely solely on the data. And so what I spend a lot of time talking to my team about is how we can balance that. So thinking about, I guess a couple general things I would say are there are right and wrong times I think for both for your gut and for data. And then there are lots of different kinds of data and different ways to use that data.
turns.zh: 然后你就发现自己陷在一个循环里：你造东西只是为了造它，而没有真正去想它和终端用户的连接。我觉得数据太神奇了，就像：我们在 Spotify 有个不可思议的洞察团队，无论是我的洞察团队，还是更大的那个。我们真的太幸运了，我们对用户、对不同群体、对他们要什么、缺什么，有那么多认知，所以我觉得那极有价值。我觉得人们踩坑的地方，是当他们以为自己可以只依赖数据。所以我花大量时间跟团队聊的，是我们怎么去平衡它。去思考——我想说几个概括性的东西吧——无论是对你的直觉、还是对数据，都有对的时机和错的时机。而数据也有许多不同的种类、许多不同的用法。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: So I think when you're in the trap of just being like, well, this is the process we always have with insights and we're just going to run this every time we have a feature, I don't think you're going to have a great time. I think if you think of it as part of the creative process as a PM where you're like, I have a hypothesis, I have some data that is helping me understand that hypothesis in the first place or form it in the first place, then I'm going to do some user research and try a couple of things and see what works for people. Then I'm going to make sure that we have success metrics and that we know what we're looking for when we launch, then we're going to follow, et cetera. So I think there's different times and places for all the different types of data collection that you can do.
turns.zh: 所以我想，当你掉进那种「嗯，这是我们做洞察一直以来的流程，每次有新功能我们就跑一遍」的陷阱时，你不会玩得开心。我想，如果你把它当成 PM 创意流程的一部分——就像：我有个假设，我有些数据，最初是帮我去理解、或者去形成那个假设的，然后我要去做些用户研究、试几样东西、看看对人们什么管用。然后我要确保我们有成功指标、知道发布时我们在找什么，然后我们会去跟进，等等。所以我想，对所有不同类型的「数据收集」，都有不同的时机和位置。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: The other thing I would say is something that I have had to learn as a leader, especially as part of a larger organization, when we were a startup Anchor was like 20 people when we got acquired by Spotify. And by the way, Spotify is my first big tech company, so I've always been at startups, so I've learned a lot about that. But when I was leading product at a startup, it's like we're a small team, we're really focused on moving quickly. There isn't a whole lot of stopping to ask what data is supporting this or it's just like we talked to some users and we're like, great, that's a problem. We're just going to go and fix it. And I think at Spotify there's obviously at places like Spotify, I mean, large organizations, there's obviously a lot more people that you need to coordinate.
turns.zh: 另一件我想说的事，是我作为领导者、尤其作为更大组织的一部分，必须去学的——Anchor 被 Spotify 收购时大概才 20 人。顺便说，Spotify 是我待过的第一家大科技公司，所以我一直都在初创里，关于那个我学了很多。但当我在初创里带产品时，就像：我们是个小团队，极度聚焦于快速推进。没那么多停下来问「什么数据在支撑这个」的时候，就只是：我们跟几个用户聊了，然后说「好，那是问题，我们直接去修」。而我想在 Spotify 这种地方——我是说，大组织——显然有多得多的、不在你直属团队里、需要你去影响的人。所以我想，我必须学的一件事是：凭直觉驱动，不等于就跟大家说「我告诉过你了、或者我相信这个，所以你们得做」。我觉得平衡它，是有门艺术的。而我想我尝试去做的是：永远尽可能客观地去解释，为什么我的直觉会是那样。就像你可以回溯到你多年的经验、或者其他类似做过的事；你可以聊你作为用户去测这个东西的体验；你可以搬出用户的故事和轶事来佐证。而我发现，那显然好用得多。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: There's a lot of people you have to influence that aren't on your immediate team. And so I think something that I've had to learn is that being gut driven isn't the same as just saying to people, I told you or I believe this, so you have to do it. There really is an art I think to balancing that. And I think that what I try to do is always still as objectively as possible explain why my gut is feeling that way. So it's like you can refer back to your years of experience or other things that you've done that have been similar. You can talk about your experience as a user testing this stuff. You can bring in stories and anecdotes from users to help back it up. And so I have found that that works obviously a lot better.
turns.zh: 而我想，在那些我这样做过、或者我见过其他领导者这样做的时刻——如果他们只是说「嗯，我们就这么做，哪怕你们不同意、或者数据说另一样」——那些项目从一开始就一定死定了。它们绝不可能成。你没法拖着所有这些人，去做一件他们自己都不信的事。所以我想，你其实该把你的直觉当成一种「数据」来看待——我觉得它是完全有效的那一种，只是你需要讲清楚你正在与之共事的就是它；然后它应该被当作和其他任何数据点一样严肃对待。所以我试着那么去想：理想中，这一切该一起协作。而显然，你有的数据越多、数据的种类越多，你就越有说服力、也越可能对。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And I think that in the times that either I have done this or I've seen other leaders do it, where they're just like, well, we're just going to do it this way even if you guys don't agree or if the data says something different, those projects are always immediately doomed from the beginning. They're never going to work. You can't drag all these people through something that they don't believe in. So I think I would think of your gut actually as a type of data and I think it's a totally valid one and it's just I think you need to be clear that that's what you're working with, but then it should be taken as seriously as any other data point. So I try and think of it that way where it's like this should all ideally work together. And obviously the more data you have and the more types of data you have, the more convincing you're going to be and the more right you're going to be.
turns.zh: 所以我想这一切都有帮助。在 Anchor 早期有太多这种时刻了，因为——我都不确定，我想我们直到并入 Spotify 才有了第一个数据科学家，所以之前大概是工程师在跑查询。但有几次，我们不得不把 Anchor 从 1.0 挪到 2.0、再从 2.0 挪到 3.0，我们做了这些大的——我不爱叫它们「转型」（pivot），但算是「演进」吧——关于我们的产品或战略。术语在你想说服人时也极其重要。所以当我思考那些我们团队的大转折时，两次我们都有那种和团队在一起的、必须让所有人上同一条船去做大改动的时刻。Anchor 1.0——我不知道你记不记得——其实有点像 Clubhouse 后来重新包装成的那种，更偏向语音消息和短内容、更关于人与人的连接。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: So I think it all helps. There were so many of these in the early days of Anchor because I don't even know, I don't think we had a data scientist until we were part of Spotify, so I think it was just engineers running queries. But there were a couple times where we had to move Anchor from 1.0 to 2.0 and then from 2.0 to 3.0, we did these big, I don't like to call them pivots, but sort of evolutions let's say, of our product or our strategy terminology also very important when you're trying to convince people of things. So when I was thinking about those big transitions for us as a team, I think both times we had these big moments with our teams where we had to get everyone on board with making these big changes. So with Anchor 1.0, I don't know if you remember, but it was actually similar to what Clubhouse I think just rebranded to more voice messaging and short form and more about connections between people.
turns.zh: 那是我们发布的第一个东西，人们爱死了。人们对它超兴奋，数据全好。留存极高。我们从用户那儿，一直听到这种种：他们熬夜在用这个 app，人们在上面相遇、相爱、甚至在我们的平台上结婚，所有这些真的像魔法一样的事；而且我们看到用户基数在稳步增长。但我想我们当时有种感觉——我说「我们」，主要是当时 Mike 和我，Mike 是我们的 CEO——就是它永远不可能大到哪儿去。所以我们经历了这个特别有趣的时刻：用户全在跟我们说「没问题啊」，他们爱这个产品，每天都在用、会回来。它在慢慢涨，而我们就像：这永远到不了我们需要它去的地方；我们最初的目标是「让音频民主化」。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And that was the first thing we ever launched and people loved it. People were very excited about it, the data was all good. We had extremely retained users. We anecdotally, we were hearing all this stuff from users all the time that they were staying up all night to use the app, people were meeting each other and falling in love and getting married on our platform, all of these really kind of magical things and we were seeing the user base was growing consistently. But I think we had this feeling, and when I say, I mean, mostly Mike and I at the time, Mike was our CEO, that it just wasn't ever going to be big enough. And so we had this really interesting moment where the users were all telling us, there's no problem. We love this product. They were using it every day, they were coming back. It was slowly growing and we were just like, this just isn't going to get us to where we need to be, our original goal had been we wanted to democratize audio.
turns.zh: 我们想把它做成「任何人都能轻松讲出自己的故事」的东西，而我们就像：如果我们一直往这个「少数人会真的、真的爱」的小众里钻，那挺好，但那真的不是我们出发时要解决的使命。所以 1.0 到 2.0 的转折，我觉得其实相当痛苦，因为对那些投入了 1.0 的人，2.0 对他们不 work。2.0 更像是内容创作、更像一个电台，更少关于讲你个人的故事和亲密关系，更多关于「广播出去」、用不同的工具。总之，我们做那个决定，我想基本上就是凭直觉——就像：这是个商业决定。这是我们认为下一阶段需要去的地方。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: We wanted to make it something where anyone could easily tell their story, and we were like, if we keep digging ourselves into this niche that a small number of people really, really love, that's great, but that's not really the mission that we sent out set out to solve. And so the 1.0 to 2.0 transition was I think actually pretty painful because for all of those people who had been invested in 1.0, 2.0 didn't work for them. 2.0 was much more about content creation and making more of a radio station, and it was less about telling your personal story and close relationships and more about projecting and using different tools. Anyway, so we made that call I think pretty much just on gut and it was like, this is a business decision. This is where we think the next phase needs to be.
turns.zh: 当我们建 Anchor 2.0 时，它更像是我们自己想用的工具，即便那不是用户群在要的。所以我想那是一个例子：有时整个用户群并不总知道该要什么，他们并不总知道你需要替他们解决什么问题。所以我觉得，你真的得能听见「背后的东西」，或者即便数据看着还行，也要去想：它正朝着你需要它去的方向走吗？

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: When we built Anchor 2.0, it was a lot more like the tools that we wanted to use, even though it wasn't what the user base was asking for. So I think that's one example of sometimes it's that whole users don't always know what to ask for, they don't always know what problems they need you to solve for them. And so I think you really have to be able to hear what's behind it or really even if the data is looking okay, think about if it's heading to where you need it to go.
turns.zh: 在你继续之前——那其实是个这么有意思的故事，因为要让一个「正在 work、人们又爱」的产品，决定彻底改掉它，太难了。很多创始人大概就卡在这儿：他们就像「嘿，这 work 啊，而且我们感觉找到了点 fit」。你从那里面还学到别的什么吗？因为在你这个案子里，那显然是个很棒的洞见，而且最后是成了的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before you move on, that's actually such an interesting story because it's so hard to have a product that's working that people love and decide to change it completely. Many founders are probably stuck in this where they're just like, hey, this is working and we're feeling some fit. Is there anything else you learned from that? Because that's a really interesting insight and it worked out in your case clearly.
turns.zh: 它绝对是成了的。我是说，我想那是个吓死人的转折。我们当时，花了大概几个月重建了整个新 app——现在要更久，但整个我们在建它的过程中，一直在想「这会不会是个错」，我们会反复摇摆，跟用户聊他们想让我们做啥时，我们还会觉得内疚。但我想，那是那种「一旦我们发布 2.0，数字就开始飙升」的事，我们开始看到更多种人在用它，人们突然用它用得像我们一直设想的——作为那种老派、极难做的传统播客的替代品。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: It absolutely worked out. I mean, I think it was a terrifying transition. Us at the time, it took us a few months to build a whole new app, it takes longer now, but the whole time we were building it, we were like, we weren't sure if it was a mistake and we would go back and forth and we would feel guilty when we were talking to our users about what they wanted us to be working on. But I think it was one of those things where as soon as we launched 2.0, our numbers started shooting up and we started seeing more kinds of people were using it and people were suddenly using it in the way that we had always imagined as a replacement for the old school, very difficult to make traditional podcasts.
turns.zh: 我不知道。我想教训就是：你得能穿过噪音听见信号，即便你有一堆大声的用户在要某个东西。我们以前有个规矩，80/20 法则——就像你不能只为了那 20% 去建；我想这不是我们发明的，应该是个常见说法，但我们总引用它说：我们要为那 80% 建，即便那 20% 会更聒亮，那只会让你更深地陷进那个「你其实不是在为所有人建」的坑里。而我想，尤其当你想建一个创意平台、想民主化某样东西、你的目标用户是地球上每个人时，你真的得愿意「杀掉你的挚爱」（kill your darlings），在它们没把你带到该去的地方时，放手。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I don't know. I guess the lesson is you have to be able to tell the signal through the noise, and even if you've got lots of vocal users asking for something, we used to have this rule, the 80/20 rule, where it's like you can't just build for that 20, I don't think we made this up by the way. I think this is a common thing, but we'd always refer to it and say, we want to be building for the 80%, and even though the 20% are going to be more vocal, that's just going to get you deeper into that hole of that problem of you're not really building for everyone. And I think particularly when you're trying to build a creative platform, you're trying to democratize something and your target user is everyone on the planet. I think you really have to be willing to kill your darlings and let things go when they're not getting where you need them to be.
turns.zh: 那大概是大多数常见的情况。某样东西在 work，但没 work 到极好。我们怎么办？所以那真的有意思。我觉得你刚才说的第一点真的很重要——我们当时有个大得多的使命和愿景，即便这个在 work，它也永远到不了那儿。没有路径去建一个巨大的生意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's probably the most common cases. Something is working, but it's not working incredibly well. What do we do? And so that's really interesting. I feel like the first thing you said there is really important of just we had a much bigger mission and vision, and even though this is working, this is never going to get there. There's no path to building a massive business.
turns.zh: 我确实觉得那太重要了，而且我把很多功劳归于 Mike 和我们的联合创始人。我想他们从公司一开局就清楚自己想做什么，而且多年来、贯穿被收购的全程，都对此极其坚定、从未动摇。所以我想，并非每个人的目标都是建一个价值数十亿、改变世界的生意——如果你的目标不是那个，那也没关系；但如果那就是你的目标，你就得咬住它，而那真的很难，但你得不断 pivot 才能到你想要的地方。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I do think that's so important, and I give a lot of credit to Mike and our co-founders. I think they really knew what they wanted to do when they started the company and they were very firm on that and never varied that throughout the years throughout the acquisition. And so I do think not everyone's goal is to build a massive multi-billion dollar world changing business, that's okay if that's not your goal, but if that is your goal, you have to stick to it and it's really hard, but you have to keep pivoting to get to where you want to be.
turns.zh: 「杀掉你的挚爱」。我爱这个说法，我整天都在用。我想你还有第二个例子。我还有几个关于 Anchor 的问题，但你想再分享一个例子吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kill your darlings. I love that phrase, I use it all the time. I think you had a second example. I have a couple other questions of Anchor, but did you want to share another example?
turns.zh: 当然，我快速说一下，我的第二个例子是：我们其实不得不又做了一次。我们从 Anchor 1.0 到 2.0，当时想「那绝对是正确的决定」。然后 Anchor 2.0，我们还处在那个阶段，总会拿它开玩笑，因为人们会说「哦，它有点像在做播客」。而我们会说：它不是播客，因为我们想比播客更大。因为在当时，2015 年，还在播客的人那么少，做播客还那么难。所以我们最初特别卡在「播客这个词会是个限制、我们想做下一个东西」这个念头里。在 Anchor 早期，我们有一整套航海术语，所以我们管它们叫 waves 之类的，别的我记不清了，但我们对一切想抵抗「播客」和「播客主」的词，都有可爱的航海叫法。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Sure, I can just quickly, my second example was, so we actually had to do it again. So we went from Anchor 1.0 to 2.0, we were like, that was totally the right call. And then Anchor 2.0, we were still in this phase where we would always joke about it because people would be like, "Oh, it's kind of like making a podcast." And we would be like, it's not a podcast because we're trying to be bigger than podcasts. Because we were at the time, 2015, there were still so few people podcasting, it was still so hard to do. And so we originally were really stuck on this idea that podcasting was going to be limiting and that we wanted to be the next thing. In the early days of Anchor, we had all this nautical terminology, so we would call them waves and I don't remember what else, but we had cute nautical terms for everything we were trying to resist podcast and podcaster and those things.
turns.zh: 而当我们发布 Anchor 2.0，开始拿到所有那些超棒的牵引力时，人们提的第一大功能需求是：他们就像「太好了，我爱用这些工具，然后我想把它导出成播客、发布出去、让人那样来听」。而我们抗拒了大概——我不知道——六个月还是多久，我们就像「绝对不，那不是我们要做的」。而我想那次是个特别有意思的教训，因为我们刚学到「不听了用户的话、做了正确的事」。所以有阵子我们掘地三尺，说「那不是我们要去的方向，他们并不知道他们真正要什么」。然后当我们决定时，我想我们是先从「哦，我们做个小测试，让人们把播客导出来，看看会怎样」开始的。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And when we launched Anchor 2.0, we started getting all of this really great traction and the number one feature requests that we got from people is they were like, great, I love using these tools and then I want to export it as a podcast and publish it and get people listening that way. And we resisted it for probably, I don't know, six months or something and we were like, absolutely not, that's not what we're doing. And I think that one was such an interesting lesson because we had just learned that we did the right thing by not listening to our users. So for a while we dug in and we were like, that's not the direction we're going in, they don't know what they actually want. And then when we decided, I think we started with like, oh, we'll do a little test and let people export us podcasts and see what happens.
turns.zh: 而当我们回头看数据时，那正是我们看到「曲棍球杆式增长」起点的时刻——我们之前一直在涨、一直做得不错，然后你拉远了看，就像：好吧，那显然就是我们缺的那块。又一次，我们不得不停下手里的事，把整个 app 重建，围绕 RSS、播客、和「能导出」来建。而且我们其实做了些很酷的事，让人们能超容易地把播客发布到各处。所以我想，那正是它起飞的时刻。而把这两件事放一起看真的很有意思，因为第二次，我们不得不放弃的，恰恰是我们曾以为「对我们的生意本质为真」的一块。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And when we look back at our data, that's the moment when we saw the beginning of that hockey stick growth where it's like we had been growing, we had been doing well, and then you zoom out and you're like, okay, that was very clearly the thing we were missing. Yet again, we had to stop what we were doing, we rebuilt the entire app, we built it around RSS and podcasting and being able to export. And we actually did some really cool things to make it really easy for people to publish their podcast everywhere. So I think that was really the moment that it took off. And I think it's so interesting putting those two things together because it was the opposite thing the second time that we had to give up on a piece of what we had thought was so inherently true about our business.
turns.zh: 所以我想，能给人的教训，除了「你得保持——尤其在初创心态里——愿意变通、愿意随着产品成熟、随着用户群变化，去吸收新信息和新数据点」之外，没有别的。会有新东西让你学到，而改变你对它的想法。而我想，再一次，对我们来说不可动摇的，就是我们的使命；其他一切对我们都是可变的——就像：无论我们需要做什么才能到那儿，都会 work。而回头看，我确实惊讶于我们当时有多勇敢——我们不断找到某种产品市场契合，然后说「不，那还不够」，然后推进到下一件事。而我想，那显然对我们极好地成了，也意味着我们得以去做出发时想做的事、真正让这个媒介民主化、为更多人把事情变容易得多。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And so I don't know what lesson to tell people to take away from that other than I think you have to just stay, especially in a startup mentality, you have to stay willing to be flexible and take in new information and new data points as your product matures and as your user base changes, there's going to be new things that you learn that are going to change how you think about it. And I think again, the one thing that was unwavering for us was our mission and everything else was mutable for us where we were like, whatever we need to do to get there will work. And I do think looking back, it's astonishing how brave we were that we kept finding some product market fit and being like, nope, that's not enough. And then moving to the next thing. And I think that obviously worked out really well for us and meant that we were able to do what we set out to do and really democratize the medium and make things a lot easier for a lot more people.
turns.zh: 而我想那里面另一个教训就是：去试。就像你说的，你试了那个导出功能，「我们就看看会怎样」。不，我们不觉得那是我们要去的方向，但我们就试一下，也许就成了。而显然，它成了产品和平台的核心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think another lesson there is just try stuff. Like you said, you tried this export thing, let's just see what happens. No, we don't think this is where we need to go, but let's just try it and maybe it'll work. And clearly that became the core of the product and platform.
turns.zh: 我想另一个教训就是去试东西。就像你说的，你试了那个导出功能，就看看会怎样。不，我们不觉得那是我们该去的方向，但就试一下，也许就成了。而显然，那成了产品与平台的核心。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Totally. And also, you never know which of those tiny product changes are going to end up being this existential moment for your business. You really have to keep your eyes open and be ready for that to happen anytime, especially when you're still trying to figure out where your place is going to be.
turns.zh: 完全同意。而且你也永远不知道那些微小的产品改动里，哪一个最终会成为你业务的生死时刻。你真的得睁大眼睛、随时准备好这种事在任何时候发生，尤其是你还忙着搞清楚自己到底要往哪儿去的时候。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned there was this feature that made it easy to distribute your podcast, and this touches on a question that actually asked Mike Mignano, the CEO of anchor what to ask you. And he's like, ask her about the story of how you made that actually possible to distribute the podcast to platforms, and it ended up being a very unscalable solution.
turns.zh: 你刚提到有个功能让播客分发变得很容易，这正好呼应了 Mike Mignano——Anchor 的 CEO——问我该问你什么问题。他说，问问她那个让播客能分发到各个平台的故事，最后发现那是个根本没法规模化的方案。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: One of our principles from the very early days of Anchor was build things that don't scale, where we were like, we're a ridiculously tiny team. We're trying to do this really big thing. We had raised very little money, and so we were always just trying to figure out how can we hack into whatever growth we're trying to make happen. So when it turned out that people wanted to distribute their podcasts everywhere, it's gotten a little bit easier. But at the time, I'm sure you remember what podcast distribution was like, where it's like there's all of these different podcast platforms you have to manually distribute to all of them. Apple Podcasts in particular can be really difficult for people who aren't tech-savvy because there's this whole, you have to prove that you own your RSS feed, you have to know what an RSS feed is.
turns.zh: Anchor 从很早时候起就有一条原则：去构建那些「不 scalability」的东西。当时我们团队小得离谱，却想做一件特别大的事，融的钱也极少，所以一直都在琢磨怎么才能 hack 出我们想要的增长。后来发现大家都想把播客分发到所有平台——现在这事儿稍微容易点儿了，但那时候，你肯定记得播客分发是什么样：一堆不同的平台，你得手动一个一个去发。尤其是 Apple Podcasts，对不怎么懂技术的人特别难，因为你要证明自己拥有那个 RSS feed，还得先知道 RSS feed 是什么。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: You have to sometimes deal with 301 redirects. There's just all this stuff that's deeply technical in a way that we were just like it doesn't need to be. And so one of the steps there was to submit your podcast to Apple Podcasts, you had to have an Apple ID, and there are a lot of people in the world who don't have iPhones, and so we're building for everybody. So we were like, how can we reduce that friction? We were obsessed with reducing friction, this was our constant battle. And so we had this idea, we hired a couple of college interns and we brought them in and we were like, people are going to push this magical one button in the Anchor app and they're going to say, I want to distribute my podcast, and your job is going to be to do all that same manual stuff manually, but to them it's going to feel magical and it happened automatically. I still don't know how many people know this.
turns.zh: 有时候你还得处理 301 重定向。全是这种极其技术化的东西，而我们一直觉得——这根本没必要这么复杂。所以在把播客提交到 Apple Podcasts 这一步，你得有个 Apple ID，可世界上很多人根本没有 iPhone，而我们是要为所有人做产品的。于是我们就想：怎么降低这个摩擦？我们 obsessed with 减少摩擦，这是一场持久战。后来我们有了个点子：雇了几个大学生实习生，把他们招进来，跟他们说，用户会在 Anchor app 里按一个神奇的按钮，说「我要分发我的播客」，而你的工作就是把那些手动步骤手动做完，但对他们来说，感觉就像魔法一样、自动就发生了。到现在我都不知道有多少人知道这事儿。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I think people think that we had some secret backdoor deal with Apple for distribution, but we just had college students making Apple podcast accounts and then submitting hundreds of thousands of podcasts through these accounts. And that resulted in lots of interesting technical and relationship situations. It was a really interesting thing, and eventually that didn't scale, eventually we stopped doing that, obviously, but I think that is such a cool example of the importance of how you're packaging what you're offering to people where if we had said you request distribution and we'll have one of our team members get back to you in three days and let you know when you're on Apple Podcasts, that doesn't feel very magical or it's really saving you any time. If all you see as a user is you're hitting a button and then 24 hours later you're somehow magically on Apple Podcasts, that was so much easier than manual distribution was at the time.
turns.zh: 我想很多人以为我们跟 Apple 有什么秘密后台交易才能分发，但其实我们只是让大学生去注册 Apple Podcasts 账号，然后通过这些账号提交了几十万个播客。这带来了不少有意思的技术和关系上的状况。这事儿挺妙的，当然最后它确实没法规模化，我们后来也就停了——但我想这是个特别好的例子，说明你「包装」自己提供给别人的东西有多重要：如果我们当时说的是「你申请分发，我们团队有人三天后回复你、告诉你上没上 Apple Podcasts」，那根本不会让人觉得神奇，也没真正帮你省时间。而用户看到的只是：按一下按钮，24 小时后你就神奇地出现在了 Apple Podcasts 上——那比当时的手动分发容易太多了。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And I think that was a really big part of why we got so much hosting market share so quickly because it was such an insane benefit over the other platforms which otherwise had been commoditized at that point. So, it's funny now to think back on that, but I think it's also related to we were so good at being willing to humor what seemed like stupid ideas and try them. And so that is something that I definitely recommend to product people is let yourself have the silly ideas we always talked about yes and when someone has an idea, how can you build on it and think about how it might work instead of saying, no, that can't work because, and so we had a number of those things where it was like nobody understood how we were doing things so differently, and it was just because we weren't afraid to do the silly unscalable thing for a while.
turns.zh: 我想这正是我们能那么快拿到那么多托管市场份额的一大原因，因为相比当时已经沦为commodity的其他平台，这是个疯狂的优势。所以现在回想起来挺好笑的，但我也觉得这跟我们特别擅长「愿意去尝试那些看起来蠢的点子」有关。所以我绝对会建议做产品的人：允许自己有那些傻点子。我们总说「yes, and」——当别人有个想法，你怎么在它上面叠加、去想它怎么可能 work，而不是说「不，那行不通，因为……」。所以我们有好些事，外人根本搞不懂我们为什么做得这么不一样，就是因为我们不害怕先去做一阵子那种傻的、没法规模化的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that story. Touches on two things, one is I was just doing an interview around how to drive word to mouth growth and make that a big driver of your growth. And the main message there is just make something remarkable and knock people's socks off that they're just like, oh wow, this is crazy, I'm going to share it with my friend. And that's such a good example of that where everyone's like, wow, that was easy, I'm going to tell all my other friends that are launching podcasts. The other is, I wonder just how much of tech is built off of college interns, the beginnings of companies or how important college interns are to technology and innovation. It feels like there's always an intern story.
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个故事。它点到两件事：一是我刚做了个关于怎么驱动口碑增长、把它变成你增长主力的访谈，那里的核心信息就是——做出让人惊叹、让人「哇」一声「这太疯了，我要分享给我朋友」的东西。而这就是个绝佳例子：大家都说「哇，这真容易，我要告诉我所有也在做播客的朋友」。另一件是，我好奇到底有多少科技公司是建立在大学实习生之上的，或者说大学实习生对科技和创新有多重要。感觉总会有一个实习生的故事。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Yeah, I know. I think they must be. And for the record, we paid them very well, these were not unpaid interns, just to be clear. But no, I think it is amazing, and I think it was also such a cool opportunity. One of those interns actually is still a PM on my team today. She ended up converting a full-time after she graduated. And I remember I had a lot of cool college internships and it's such a cool way to get exposure to industries that you otherwise wouldn't get to. So I would definitely recommend that college kids start with, it's okay if your first job is like a repetitive, not very exciting thing. If you do a good job, it will lead to something very exciting maybe.
turns.zh: 对，我知道。我觉得肯定是这样。而且说清楚一下，我们给的薪酬很好，这些不是无偿实习生。不过不，我觉得这太棒了，而且它也是个超棒的机会。其中一个实习生到现在还在我团队里当 PM。她毕业后转成了全职。我记得我自己也做过不少很酷的大学实习，那是接触你本来接触不到的行业的一种特别酷的方式。所以我绝对会建议大学生：没关系，你的第一份工作可以是重复性的、没那么刺激的。只要你做得好，它会通向某种很令人兴奋的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Imagine a place where you can find all your potential customers and get your message in front of them in a cost-efficient way. If you're a B2B business, that place exists, and it's called LinkedIn. LinkedIn ads allows you to build the right relationships, drive results, and reach your customers in a respectful environment. Two of my portfolio companies, Webflow and Census, are LinkedIn success stories. Census had a 10x increase in pipeline with a LinkedIn startup team for Webflow after ramping up on LinkedIn and Q4, they had the highest marketing source revenue quarter to date. With LinkedIn ads you'll have direct access to and can build relationships with decision makers including 950 million members, 180 million senior execs and over 10 million C-level executives. You'll be able to drive results with targeting and measurement tools built specifically for B2B. In tech, LinkedIn generated two to 5x higher return on ad spend than any other social media platforms.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这点。想象一个地方，你能以高性价比找到所有潜在客户、把你的信息送到他们面前。如果你是 B2B 企业，这个地方存在，它叫 LinkedIn。LinkedIn 广告让你建立对的合作关系、驱动结果、在一个彼此尊重的环境里触达你的客户。我的两家被投公司 Webflow 和 Census 都是 LinkedIn 的成功案例。Census 在 LinkedIn 初创团队帮助下 pipeline 增长了 10 倍；Webflow 在 Q4 加大 LinkedIn 投入后，拿到了迄今为止营销来源收入最高的一个季度。通过 LinkedIn 广告，你能直接触达并与决策者建立关系，包括 9.5 亿会员、1.8 亿高管和超 1000 万 C 级高管。你能用专为 B2B 打造的定向与衡量工具驱动结果。在科技领域，LinkedIn 的广告支出回报率比其他任何社交媒体平台高 2 到 5 倍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Audiences on LinkedIn have two times the buying power of the average web audience, and you'll work with a partner who respects the B2B world you operate in make B2B marketing everything it can be and get $100 credit on your next campaign. Just go to linkedin.com/podlenny to claim your credit. That's linkedin.com/podlenny. Terms and conditions apply. So we've been talking about Anchor and I think what's really interesting about Anchor is it's one of the very rare success stories of an acquisition working out incredibly well. It was a small startup now powering two thirds of all new podcasts. It's pretty insane. So I want to spend a little time on just what worked in making that possible. So let me ask first around the integration piece, just how you integrated successfully, and then I want to talk about just operationalizing and making it continue running successfully.
turns.zh: LinkedIn 上的受众购买力是普通网页受众的两倍，而且你会和一个尊重你所处 B2B 世界的伙伴合作——让 B2B 营销发挥全部潜力，并在你下一轮 campaign 拿到 $100 信用额度。只要去 linkedin.com/podlenny 领取你的信用额度。就是 linkedin.com/podlenny。条款与条件适用。我们一直在聊 Anchor，而我觉得 Anchor 真正有意思的地方在于，它是收购结果好得惊人的极少数案例之一。它曾是个小初创，如今驱动着所有新播客的三分之二。这相当疯狂。所以我想花点时间聊聊，到底是什么让这成为可能。先问整合这一块——你是怎么成功整合的——然后我想聊聊怎么把它运营化、让它持续成功运转。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So on the first piece, just what did you do right to integrate Anchor into Spotify to make it effective and continue working?
turns.zh: 好。那第一块，为了让 Anchor 融入 Spotify 并发挥作用、持续运转，你做对了什么？

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I think it's a combination of luck and hard work because Spotify is genuinely an amazing company. I mean, you've met now a bunch of people who I work with at Spotify, including my boss, Gustav. It's an incredible company. They're Swedish. So just their mindset about everything in the first place is amazing. But also, I have been so impressed that they are the type of company that can still move quickly and make really big strategic decisions and strategic shifts. It never feels like they're slowing down. And so I think our way of working worked with them. And then I think the other thing that we had to our benefit was they really saw the same vision that we had. So it was like they also wanted to change podcasting and make it more democratized and make it more two-way and bring it into the future.
turns.zh: 我想是运气加努力的结合，因为 Spotify 真的是家了不起的公司。你现在已经见过好几个我在 Spotify 的同事了，包括我老板 Gustav。它是家不可思议的公司。他们是瑞典人，所以他们对一切的心智模式从根上就很棒。但同样让我印象极深的是，他们是那种还能快速行动、做出真正重大的战略决策和战略转向的公司。从来不让人觉得他们在慢下来。所以我想我们的工作方式跟他们合得来。然后另一个对我们有利的点是，他们真的看到了和我们一样的愿景。也就是他们也想改变播客、让它更民主化、更双向、把它带向未来。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And it was so interesting because when we started talking to them, both of us had this chicken or egg marketplace problem where we had this critical mass of creators. They had a critical mass at that point of consumers, but if you don't have both on the same place, then you're still stuck with the limitations of RSS feeds. And so I think we were both coming at the acquisition with the same frustration just from two different angles. And so both of us really saw that benefit in joining up. And so I think one of the big ways we were lucky is that what I've seen happen in a lot of acquisitions is you have an idea of what you're getting acquired for and you get excited and really attached to that vision, and then when that vision doesn't end up fitting into the company strategy, there's nowhere else to go.
turns.zh: 特别有意思的是，我们刚开始跟他们谈的时候，两边都有这个鸡生蛋蛋生鸡的双边市场问题：我们有一群关键的创作者，他们在那会儿有一群关键的消费者，但如果你两边不在同一个地方，你就还是被 RSS feed 的局限卡住。所以我想我们是从同一个挫败出发来谈收购的，只是角度不同。于是我们双方都清楚合并的好处。所以我想我们能走运的一大原因是：我看到很多收购里，你对自己被收购是为了什么有个设想，你会兴奋、会死死附着在那个愿景上，然后当那个愿景最终跟公司战略不吻合时，你就没别的地方可去了。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And I think in a lot of ways Anchor did really well fit into Spotify's culture and their roadmap, but there were many things that changed around that initial vision. And I think we were really good at making sure that we stayed valuable to Spotify. That was one of our goals when we got acquired where we were like, we're tiny startup people, and we're like, we're not going to get lost in this big sea. When we came in, it was like we were very vocal about everything that we were doing, we did lots of internal marketing and made sure people were excited. We built a lot of really strong relationships. We made sure that every team at Spotify knew about us and what we were doing. We were constantly asking how we could help other teams. And when the strategy shifted, which it has dozens of times since we've gotten acquired almost five years ago, not like we just blindly followed, but we were always willing to get excited about whatever the next thing was and willing to be helpful and figure out how to make that work.
turns.zh: 而我想在很多层面上，Anchor 确实很好地融入了 Spotify 的文化和路线图，但围绕那个最初愿景，有很多东西变了。而我觉得我们很擅长确保自己一直对 Spotify 有价值。这是我们被收购时的目标之一——我们当时想，我们是 tiny startup 的人，我们说，我们不会在这片大海里迷失。我们进来时，对自己的所作所为非常张扬，做了大量内部营销、确保大家兴奋起来。我们建立起了很多很强的关系。我们确保每个 Spotify 的团队都知道我们和我们在做什么。我们不断问自己能怎么帮到其他团队。而自从大约五年前被收购以来，战略已经转了无数次了——不是说我们盲目跟随，而是我们总是愿意对下一件事物兴奋起来、愿意帮忙、去想怎么让它 work。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And I think it actually goes back to the sticking to the mission in the first place where Spotify and we want podcasting to be able to be a huge business for the industry. We think it's been held back by a lot of things for a long time. And so we've had various hypotheses about how we can get there and we try things and if something doesn't work, we go onto the next thing. But that goal hasn't really changed.
turns.zh: 我想这其实又回到了最开始「坚守使命」这点上：Spotify 和我们，都希望播客能成为这个行业里一门巨大的生意。我们认为它长期以来被很多东西拖了后腿。所以我们有过各种关于怎么到达那里的假说，我们去试，不行就换下一件。但这个目标基本没变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes a lot of sense. And I love the idea of just staying excited about what is happening. I think a lot of founders join and they're like, "Oh, it's so annoying to work in this big company." "Oh man, we have this original plan, it's just not happening." And I think even if you're probably not, even if you're not excited, I think it's effective to communicate that you're excited and be on board and then shift things in what direction you think maybe needs to go instead.
turns.zh: 这很有道理。而且我喜欢「对正在发生的事保持兴奋」这个想法。我想很多创始人在加入大公司后会说：「哦，在大公司干活真烦。」「天呐，我们原来的计划根本没发生。」而我想，哪怕你可能并不兴奋，表现出兴奋、表示你站在船上、然后把你觉得该走的方向慢慢挪过去，这本身是有效的。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Totally, yeah.
turns.zh: 完全同意，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And then in terms of operating within Spotify, from what I understand, your team is still very startupy and there's this really fast moving mentality. What have you learned and how do you do that? How do you make that happen within a larger company?
turns.zh: 好。那在 Spotify 内部运营方面，据我所知，你的团队依然很有 startup 范儿，保持着这种快速移动的 mentality。你学到了什么？你是怎么做到的？在大公司里怎么让这个发生？

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: We've definitely slowed down a little, I will say. I'm always joking about when we first got acquired, I remember we had to do this spreadsheet outlining our roadmap and estimate are things like small, extra large, whatever, and Spotify's definition of small with something like a quarter. And I was like, we've never built anything that took more than three months. And now it's like now we build lots of things to take more than three months. But the first thing that comes to mind, so when we were a startup, one of the first things we did when we were only a few people, we decided what our core values were going to be. And I think they maybe very trivially have changed over the years, but we essentially still have the same four core values that we decided on seven or eight years ago now. And when we got acquired, we had a conversation with our team where we said, we're going to of course embrace Spotify's culture and Spotify's core values, but we're not going to forget who we are as a team.
turns.zh: 我得说，我们确实慢下来一点了。我总开玩笑说，刚被收购时，我记得我们得填一张表、列出路线图，估算事情是小、超大还是怎样，而 Spotify 对「小」的定义是大概一个季度。我当时说，我们从来没花超过三个月做过任何东西。而现在，我们会做很多要花超过三个月的事。但我脑子里蹦出来的第一件事是：我们还是 startup 的时候，在只有几个人的时候，就定下了我们的核心价值观。我想这些年它们可能只改了一丁点，但我们现在用的，基本还是七八年前定的那四条核心价值观。被收购时，我们跟团队聊过：我们当然会拥抱 Spotify 的文化和价值观，但我们不会忘了自己作为一个团队是谁。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And I think part of what really... And one of our core values by the way, is move fast. So that's something that's very deep within our DNA. But I think one of the things that helped with that is Daniel Eck, when we got acquired, came and talked to our team, which was so cool and so motivational. And one of the things he said to us was, we had a reputation at the time for moving very quickly, even compared to other startups. We were shipping a new feature every two weeks, it was insane. And Daniel said to us, not only do I want you to not move slower, that's part of why we're acquiring you so that you can move quickly. But he said, I also want you to help me teach the rest of Spotify how to move more quickly, and I found that so motivating.
turns.zh: 我想真正起作用的一点……顺带一提，我们的一条核心价值观就是「move fast（快速行动）」。所以这是深植于我们 DNA 里的东西。但我觉得真正帮到这点的，是 Daniel Ek 在我们被收购时来跟我们团队讲话——那太酷、太鼓舞人心了。他对我们说的其中一句话是，我们当时以行动快闻名，哪怕跟其他 startup 比也是。我们每两周就发一个新功能，简直疯了。而 Daniel 对我们说，我不但要你们别慢下来——这正是我收购你们的原因，这样你们才能快——他还说，我也希望你们帮我教会 Spotify 其他部门怎么更快行动。我听了特别受激励。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Because I think I definitely had that feeling going from startup to larger organization where I had this fear that it was just going to be bureaucracy and things moving so slowly. And I really loved that. That was one of his goals was that he was like, I want to make sure Spotify also grew really quickly and he was trying to figure out how to help them keep moving as quickly as they used to. And so I think that's something that I really took to heart and that I've continued to remind my team of even to this day where I think of that as part of my job here to help people think about how we can move quickly and what really matters. And I think at any large organization, there's obviously a lot more complexities, there's a lot more stakeholders.
turns.zh: 因为我想我从 startup 进到大组织时，确实有过那种恐惧，觉得接下来就是官僚主义和一切慢如蜗牛。而我真的爱死了那点。他的目标之一就是：我想确保 Spotify 也能很快地成长，他在琢磨怎么帮他们保持过去那种速度。所以我想这是我真正放在心上、直到今天还在不断提醒团队的事——我把这当作我在这里工作的一部分：帮大家想清楚怎么能快、什么才是真正重要的。而我想任何大组织里，显然复杂度高得多，stakeholder 也多得多。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: So to some extent it's necessary to slow down and be thoughtful. But I think the things that I always try to push people on is the unnecessary things that slow you down. So I think that's what we spend a lot of time on, both within our team and when we're collaborating with other teams at Spotify because we work with basically everyone at this point. So I think that was really cool that he gave us that mission when we joined.
turns.zh: 所以在某种程度上，慢下来、想清楚是必要的。但我想我一直push大家去做那些「没必要的」拖慢你的事。所以我们花很多时间在这上面，不管是在我们团队内部，还是跟 Spotify 其他团队合作的时候——因为我们现在基本跟所有人都合作。所以我觉得他给我们这个使命真的特别酷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On that note, is there anything that has been a real challenge or become really annoying? Just real talk about the flip side of that. Everyone's always like, "Oh, it's all working out great." Is there anything you could share that's just like, "Oh wow, that was really hard and we overcame it, or a real challenge that we didn't expect?"
turns.zh: 顺着这点，有没有什么真的成了挑战、或者变得真的很烦的？就说点真心话，聊聊反面。大家总说「哦，一切都好得不得了」，有没有什么你能分享的，比如「哇，那真的很难、我们克服了它」，或者一个我们没预料到的真实挑战？

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I think that the downside of Daniel's advice, so one of the things he said to us, he was literally say no to all the meetings. You're going to get invited to all these off sites and meetings and everyone's going to want to meet you guys and they're going to want you to come to all of these events and whatever. And he was like, just keep being Anchor. Just keep doing what you're doing for at least the next year. Don't worry about what Spotify's doing. And on the one hand, of course, we loved that as startup people we're like, cool, we're going to get to stay us within this larger organization. But the downside that we didn't really realize until a year later was that we weren't really able to build relationships. We had some culture problems where our team started to feel like because they weren't part of Spotify, they had some existential, they didn't feel attached to the work that we were doing.
turns.zh: 我想 Daniel 那条建议的反面在于：他对我们说的其中一句话，字面上就是「对所有会议都说不」。你们会被邀请去各种 off-site、各种会议，所有人都想见你们、想让你们来参加各种活动什么的。而他说，就继续做 Anchor，至少接下来一年继续做你们在做的事，别管 Spotify 在干嘛。一方面，作为 startup 的人我们当然爱死了——酷，我们能在更大的组织里保持我们自己。但那个我们直到一年后我才真正意识到的 downside 是：我们其实没能建立起关系。我们当时有些文化问题，团队开始觉得，因为他们不属于 Spotify，他们有种存在主义式的……他们没觉得跟我们在做的事有多大归属感。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And so for a year we operated on our own. We moved really quickly, we were able to get a lot done, but then I think our next phase had to be really deeply incorporating into Spotify. And so we stopped calling our team Anchor internally, we started collaborating more with other teams. And I think that is the necessary trade-off is the more deeply you're embedded, the slower things are going to go. But I think that has been really amazing for making sure that our team actually felt like a part of the larger mission that Spotify was doing. And the one other thing I'll say that I found pretty striking. So, Spotify, as you know, did a lot of podcast acquisitions soon after the Anchor one. And so I got to know a lot of the other founders and early employees who have been acquired by Spotify and something that I've found with them and just with other acquired founders who I've talked to since, I don't know, I feel like people don't talk about this enough publicly.
turns.zh: 所以整整一年我们都自己单干。我们动得很快，干成了很多事，但我想我们的下一个阶段就必须是真正深度融入 Spotify。于是我们内部不再叫自己 Anchor 团队，开始跟其他团队合作得更多。我想那是个必要的权衡：你嵌得越深，事情就会走得越慢。但我想这点对确保我们团队真的觉得自己是 Spotify 更大使命的一部分，起了惊人的好作用。还有另一件事我觉得挺震撼的。你知道，Spotify 在收购 Anchor 之后很快又做了很多播客收购。所以我认识了很多其他被 Spotify 收购的创始人和早期员工——从我跟他们、以及后来我聊过的其他被收购创始人身上，我发现了一件事，我不知道，我觉得大家公开场合聊这个不够。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Maybe people are somewhere and I just haven't seen it. I think that people who get acquired, especially founders, actually go through a relatively deep depression and existential crisis after getting acquired. And I never would've thought, when you're talking to people about getting acquired, it sounds like such an obvious positive. Like you said, it's like this amazing positive exit and it was objectively so good for our team and for us and for our users, and I think for the industry. And I personally did not expect to go through that. Because I was like of course you want an exit, that's what you're working towards that whole time that you're a startup. And I've talked to a lot of these founders and I think it is a process I think that everyone has to go through because either you decide I'm going to stay here and I'm going to do this for a long time and I can make this work for me.
turns.zh: 也许有人在聊而我没看到。但我想，被收购的人，尤其是创始人，在收购之后其实会经历一段相当深的抑郁和存在主义危机。我以前绝不会想到——当你跟别人聊被收购，听起来那明明是个显而易见的积极事件。就像你说的，那是个惊人的正向退出，而且客观上对我们的团队、对我们自己、对我们的用户、对整个行业都极好。而我个人完全没想到自己会经历那个。因为我会想，你当然想要退出啊，那可是你做 startup 那整段时间都在奔着去的东西。而我跟很多这样的创始人聊过，我想那是个每个人都要走的过程，因为要么你决定「我要留下来、长期做下去、我能把它变成对我有利的事」，

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Or you're like, I'm just a startup founder and this doesn't really work for me and I'm going to go do my next thing. And so I think to some extent some of the things we were talking about, I think do help shake out whether people actually want to make those investments and figure out how to make things work at a big company. But I think the other thing that I've found is just I think there isn't enough support for that transition. And I think that for me, I've definitely landed on the side of, I love working at Spotify. I now am so excited to be part of a large organization and building things at this scale, but I really would've loved to been able to talk to someone about it or understand that there were other people going through that kind of thing.
turns.zh: 要么你就是「我是个 startup 创始人，这玩意儿对我不太 work，我要去做我的下一件」。所以我想在某种程度上，我们刚才聊的那些事，确实有助于厘清人们到底想不想做那些投入、去想怎么在大公司里把事情做成。但我想我发现的另一件事是：对这种过渡的支持真的太少了。而对我来说，我显然落到了「我爱在 Spotify 工作」这一边。我现在对成为大组织的一员、在这个规模上做东西，感到无比兴奋，但我真的希望能有个人可以聊聊这个，或者能明白还有别人也在经历这种事。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: So I don't know if you want an example of how it's not all rainbows and sunshine, I definitely think there were some dark times there and I've since learned everyone goes through that just because I think just by definition, all the reasons that you start a company, that means your personality is someone who wants to be having that direct impact and having your own ownership and being able to make things move quickly, and that is just so different once you join a large organization.
turns.zh: 所以如果你想要一个「它不全是阳光彩虹」的例子，我绝对觉得那里有过一段黑暗时光，而且我后来才知道大家都会经历那个——只因为，按定义来说，你当初创办公司的所有那些理由，都意味着你的性格是个想要那种直接影响力、想要自己拥有所有权、能够很快推动事情的人，而一旦你加入大组织，那一切都太不一样了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and those are amazing examples. I think what's interesting with startup life is eventually if things work out well, you'll either end up working for a larger company, that's a likely scenario if things tip go great or you're running a public company, which is also extremely painful and stressful.
turns.zh: 对，那些都是很棒的例子。我觉得 startup 生活有意思的地方在于，最终如果一切顺利，你要么会去一家更大的公司工作——如果发展特别好，这是很可能的情形——要么你会去运营一家上市公司，那也同样极度痛苦、极度有压力。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Yes, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So, the paths are hard no matter what you end up doing, as much as you love that startup time. I actually went through the same thing when we sold our company to Airbnb. I was just like, man, I had this life goal of starting a company and now I've done it and now what do I do? And it was just like, huh, okay, I guess I got to figure it out.
turns.zh: 是的。所以不管你最后做什么，路都难走，哪怕你再爱那段 startup 时光。其实我们把自己的公司卖给 Airbnb 时，我也经历了同样的事。我当时就想，天呐，我的人生目标是创办一家公司，现在做到了，然后呢？然后就愣住了，好吧，我猜我得自己想清楚。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Right? It's like, who am I? And I think the thing that I think for me, and it sounds similar to you, I think I didn't realize how much value I put in the actual day-to-day of survival that comes with being part of a startup. That becomes almost your reason for being is like, I got to make this work and I got to keep the team motivated. And you're just going, going, going, and then when everything is suddenly stable, you're like, wait, what is my job now?
turns.zh: 对吧？就是「我是谁？」。而我想，对我来说——听起来跟你也像——我之前没意识到，我把多少价值放在了「作为 startup 一员、那种日常的求生感」上。那几乎成了你存在的理由：我得把这事做成、我得让团队保持干劲。你就是不停地冲、冲、冲，然后突然一切都稳定了，你就愣住：等等，我现在的工作是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I saw a tweet actually recently, I forget who tweeted this, that CEOs that exit and go on vacation end up being more stressed and less healthy than running a really high stress, high growth company.
turns.zh: 我前阵子还真看到一条 tweet，忘了谁发的：那些退出后去度假的 CEO，比运营一家高压、高增长公司时更焦虑、更不健康。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: That is wild. I get it though.
turns.zh: 那太 wild 了。不过我懂。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Although I will say when I joined Airbnb and was just the PM of our team working on one thing, it was like, this is really cool. I don't have to worry about everything all the time, there's a really nice relief to that. But yeah, there's a life existential question of just like, wow, we did the thing. What am I? What else? There's usually not a goal beyond that.
turns.zh: 是的。不过我得说，当我加入 Airbnb、只是当个负责一件事的 PM 时，那感觉挺酷的。我不用全天候操心所有事，那种如释重负感很舒服。但确实有一个存在主义式的人生问题：「哇，我们做到了那件事。我是什么？还有什么？」通常那之外是没有目标的。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was it for you? Was it that, was it the feeling of I had this thing that I was running and now I don't?
turns.zh: 对你来说那是什么？是那种「我曾经在运行一个属于自己的东西，现在没有了」的感觉吗？

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I think it was a little bit the fear of being like a cog in a wheel, which is not actually how I feel now that I work at Spotify. And I think the other was like we were doing great, we already were killing it at podcast hosting. And also it was just so fun. I really valued that small company, everyone knows each other. We're doing really hard work, but we're also having so much fun. And I think it felt like I couldn't translate that to a large organization where I was like, okay, now I have to do things how they do. And then I think what actually ended up happening is I actually love how Spotify runs their company and I'm still able to run my team the way that works for me. And so I think it just goes back to knowing what you care about, being really solidly attached to your own core values and being able to take that with you.
turns.zh: 我想有一部分是怕变成「轮子上的一个齿轮」——而我现在在 Spotify 工作，其实并不这么觉得。另一部分是：我们当时做得很好，播客托管已经杀疯了。而且那真的很好玩。我特别看重那种小公司、彼此都认识的氛围。我们做着很难的活，但也玩得特别开心。而我觉得当时就像——我没法把那种感觉平移到大组织里，好像「好吧，现在我就得按他们的方式来」。后来真正发生的是，我其实很喜欢 Spotify 运营公司的方式，而且我依然能用对我 work 的方式带我的团队。所以我想这又回到了「知道自己看重什么、牢牢附着于你自己的核心价值观、并能够把它带在身上」。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think we're both examples of people that were startup people and then realized it's not so bad working at a big company. I stayed at Airbnb for seven years. I was like, no, no way, I'm going to be here for more than a year and a half or a year or two. How long have you been at Spotify? At this point?
turns.zh: 我想我们俩都是这样的例子：先是 startup 的人，然后发现「在大公司工作也没那么糟」。我在 Airbnb 待了七年。我当时想的是，不，我才不会待超过一年半、或者一两年。你在 Spotify 待多久了？到现在？

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: I'm going on five years. Yeah.
turns.zh: 快五年了。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, I think this is just a example of it's you think you're not going to enjoy working at a larger company, but oftentimes it's actually pretty great for a lot of different reasons.
turns.zh: 不，我想这正好说明：你以为自己不会喜欢在大公司工作，但往往其实相当不错，原因有很多。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Shifting in a slightly different direction, just thinking about leadership and what you've learned to lead teams, lead large orgs, build products, is there any just, I don't know, frameworks or tools that you found to be effective?
turns.zh: 稍微换个方向，聊聊领导力，以及你学到的怎么带团队、带大组织、做产品——有没有什么框架或工具你觉得特别有效？

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: The big one for me is Radical Candor. And I know my team watching this is going to laugh at me because I talk about this every day. They're tired of hearing it, but have you read it?
turns.zh: 对我来说是头号大事的，是《Radical Candor》（绝对坦率）。我知道我团队里看这个的人会笑我，因为我天天都在讲。他们听腻了，但你读过吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have. I love it.
turns.zh: 我读过。我爱它。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: Yeah. It's my all time favorite book. And I think it really shifted for me, honestly how I relate to people in general. But I think especially with managing, giving feedback, being able to collaborate and push back in a direct way, direct and constructive way on peers and that sort of thing. So I make all of my managers on my team read it. We talk about it constantly in our team, and I think that the general concepts for anyone who's not familiar is you need to care personally and challenge directly. And if you're only doing one of those things, you're not giving feedback in an effective way. And the book just talks so much about the importance of feedback and how feedback is a gift, which I have now come to completely agree with. It's like anytime I've given someone effective feedback, it's always well received, even if it's tough to hear, people want to get better and they want to know how they can improve.
turns.zh: 对。那是我有史以来最喜欢的书。老实说，它真的改变了我——广义上我怎么跟人打交道。但尤其是管理、给反馈、能够以直接且建设性的方式跟同侪 push back 之类的。所以我让团队里所有经理都读它。我们在团队里不停地聊它。我想对不熟悉的人，核心概念是：你得「personal care（真心关怀）」且「direct challenge（直接挑战）」。如果你只做其中一件，那你的反馈就不到位。《Radical Candor》还大谈反馈的重要性、以及「反馈是一份礼物」——这一点我现在完全同意。任何时候我给别人有效的反馈，对方总是能接受，哪怕不好听，人们都想变得更好、都想知道自己能怎么改进。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And so I think anytime that you can give them specific feedback in a way that makes it clear that you care about them and want them to be able to reach their goals, I think it makes them stronger, it makes your relationship stronger. And I also think the one other big thing I took away from Radical Candor was when it comes to people not underperforming, it really reframed how I think about that because people are not generally inherently bad or lazy or ineffective, it's almost always because the role they're in is the wrong fit. And so being able to approach the conversation in that way means that you can come at it and in a caring way that lets them know you actually want them to be successful.
turns.zh: 所以我想任何时候，你能用一种让人清楚感受到你关心他们、想让他们达成目标的方式来给具体反馈，那都会让他们更强、让你的关系更强。还有我从《Radical Candor》里学到的另一件大事是关于「人表现不佳」这件事——它完全重塑了我对此的看法，因为人一般并不是天生就差、懒、或无效，几乎总是因为他们所处的角色不匹配。所以能用这种方式去开启对话，意味着你能以一种关怀的姿态去说，让对方知道你其实是希望他们成功的。

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: And what I found is when you have the conversation in that way, they're much more receptive to it. And then you're able to either actually resolve the issues or you're able to help them figure out what the right fit is for them, which I think as a manager, it's so inspiring to me because that means that you get to keep mentoring them beyond. You're not just saying, this isn't working, I'm giving up on you, see you later. You're saying, I'm committed to helping you throughout your whole career and let's help you find the next step, even if that isn't on my team or at this company.
turns.zh: 而我发现，当你用那种方式去聊，他们会接受得多。然后你要么真的能解决问题，要么能帮他们搞清楚什么才是适合他们的位置——我觉得作为经理，这太鼓舞我了，因为这意味着你能在他们之后的人生里继续做他们的导师。你不是只说「这不行，我放弃你了，拜拜」，你是说「我致力于在你整个职业生涯里帮你，我们来帮你找到下一步，哪怕那不在我团队、也不在这家公司」。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Yeah, I love that book. And you talked about the two. There's this grid that-
turns.zh: 太棒了。是的，我爱那本书。你刚聊到那两个，书里有个 grid——

turns.speaker: Maya Prohovnik
turns.en: The quadrants?
turns.zh: 那几个象限？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it talks about. And just to reinforce what you just said, the core is that when you want to give people direct feedback, but you want to make it clear you care deeply about them. And I love that she talks about if you do one of these wrong, here's what happens.
